I want to start Phase 5. Here is a quick outcome of some brainstorming. Just internalize and wait for my next prompt for details. Not expecting any sustantive response to this prompt

___________________
✅ Agreed / decided 

Build the agent-platform capabilities once as a shared, reusable layer, pilot on mcp-agent (Phase 1 refill-triage agent — it already has the conversational shape), then carry to the Phase 2 claims stack.
Phase 5 is It's its own phase, NOT folded into Phase 2. Reasons settled: the "Phase 2 is cloud-ready" premise contradicts our documented cloud-delivery gap; this work is cloud-agnostic anyway; the conversational surface you described is Phase 1's agent; reopening a completed phase repeats the status-truthfulness problem; these are shared-platform capabilities.
Agent is becoming clinician-facing → the heavy tier (policy + judge, M6) is justified.
PHI-off-third-party = a future business rule → build the provider seam now, keep Anthropic the only live backend for now; target providers are Anthropic + Llama + DeepSeek.
Provider abstraction = two adapters only: Anthropic (native) + OpenAI-compatible (covers Llama, DeepSeek, Ollama, vLLM, and hosted endpoints). Llama-vs-DeepSeek becomes config, not code.
Output safety is a MUST: tool-with-enum-output + code validation + fail-closed to REVIEW.
policy.md into the system prompt — NOT RAG. RAG only for a genuine knowledge base, kept separate.
LLM-as-judge only for "important" responses, checking soft qualities; code enforces hard invariants.
Build order (by dependency, not your 1–5): M1 enum-gate → M2 OTel → M3 memory/context+session store → M4 deploy resilience+cost alerts → M5 provider abstraction → M6 policy+knowledge+judge. Minimal cut = M1 + M2.
Cheap Llama/DeepSeek testing: stub OpenAI-compatible server ($0 CI) / Ollama local ($0, weak — good adversary for the enum gate) / hosted OpenAI-compatible like DeepSeek API/OpenRouter/Groq (pennies, real quality).

🟡 Open issues to be brainstormed

Exact enum set for the pilot surface (dispense / review / don't-dispense is the shape; confirm the set and how REVIEW is the fail-closed sink).
Definition of an "important" response that triggers the judge.
Session-store tech (Redis vs Postgres — tie to existing infra) and where the shared platform layer lives (new agent-platform/ package vs in-place refactor).
Memory token-budget numbers — deliberately deferred until M2 metrics exist so they're set from data, not guessed.
Conversational transport — CLI REPL today; is the clinician surface a web/chat UI or API? (drives streaming + session design).
M6 RAG corpus (formulary? drug info?) or defer RAG entirely.
Phase number/name — a docs/phase5/ readiness-assessment already exists; confirm this is Phase 5 vs Phase 6, and whether the observability slice formally closes Phase 2's unbuilt R15.
_______________________________________

addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. When calling, specify search breadth: "quick" for a single targeted lookup, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" to search across multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

---
name: phase5-agent-hardening
description: "Phase 5 scoping — agent-tier productionization (memory, observability, multi-provider, follow-ups, output-safety); planning only, not yet built."
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: bebf7ac2-4f1b-4a70-8685-440da76db7e1
  modified: 2026-08-02T02:50:37.886Z
---

Planning an **agent-platform-hardening** phase (naturally Phase 5 — Phase 4/epic-emulator is
done; `docs/phase5/` holds only a readiness-assessment; branch `docs/phase5-readiness-assessment`).
Read-only/brainstorm stage — no code, no repo writes yet. User will ask for a **comprehensive
report after several milestones land** — prepare topic-4 down to code snippets especially.

Five topics the work must cover (user's numbering):
1. **Memory** — separate three axes: per-conversation token budget (cap+compact, not "autoscale"),
   concurrent-session count (real autoscale = compute), cross-session persistence store. Note:
   `MAX_TOKENS=1024` in [agent.py] is the OUTPUT cap, not memory. No memory mgmt exists today.
2. **Deploy + observability** — bounded queue + deadline (avoid queue-of-doom) as client-side
   token-bucket in front of the rate-limited/paid Anthropic API; Grafana needs metrics pipeline
   first; rate/cost ALERTS not auto-shed (clinical). 
3. **Observability (full)** — OTel: run=trace, model/tool calls=spans, `gen_ai.*` attributes,
   propagate traceID INTO claims/triage/fhir, PHI-redaction of span attrs. Strongest/most natural ask.
4. **Follow-ups + multi-model** — Meta=Llama, DeepSeek(V3/R1). Self-host via vLLM/TGI/Ollama,
   OpenAI-compatible. Real driver = PHI-off-third-party (future business rule), NOT cost.
5. **Output safety** — policy.md into system prompt (NOT RAG — rules always apply); RAG only for a
   real knowledge base; multi-model LLM-as-judge on "important" responses (code enforces hard rules,
   judge checks soft); MUST limit final answer to N enums via tool-with-enum-output + code validation
   + fail-closed to REVIEW. This is the fail-closed thesis applied to agent OUTPUT.

Proposed build order (dependency, not user's 1-5): M1 enum-gate (cheap, first, safety) · M2 OTel
foundation (the lens) · M3 memory/context+session store · M4 deploy resilience+cost alerts+Grafana ·
M5 provider abstraction (2 adapters only: Anthropic native + OpenAI-compatible covering Llama/DeepSeek/
Ollama/vLLM/hosted) · M6 policy+knowledge+judge. Minimal cut = M1+M2.

Cheap testing of Llama/DeepSeek: stub OpenAI-compatible server ($0 CI) / Ollama local ($0, weak — good
adversary for enum gate) / hosted OpenAI-compat like DeepSeek API/OpenRouter/Groq (pennies, real quality).

**KEY UNRESOLVED SCOPING DEBATE:** User proposed folding all this into **Phase 2** (adding milestones
to it), reasoning Phase 2 is "more cloud-ready." I pushed back hard: (a) that premise contradicts our
own [[cloud-delivery-gap]] docs — Phase 2 has cloud *design* but no root Terraform, not deployable;
(b) cloud-readiness is irrelevant — this work is local/cloud-agnostic; (c) the clinician-facing
conversational surface the user describes (patient/med disambiguation, dispense/review/hold) is the
**Phase 1 mcp-agent (refill triage)**, NOT Phase 2's claims-agent (which only *explains* adjudication);
(d) reopening completed-and-tagged Phase 2 repeats the status-truthfulness problem the reviewer caught;
(e) these are SHARED-PLATFORM capabilities (build once, reuse across agents like client/clinical).
Counter-proposal: own phase + shared reusable layer + scope first pass to ONE agent + defer Phase 3/4
explicitly. Observability slice arguably finishes Phase 2's unbuilt **R15**.
**OPEN QUESTION to user:** which agent is the clinician surface — (a) mcp-agent/Phase1, (b) new/evolved
claims-agent/Phase2, (c) both, platform-first then pilot on (a). My read: (c) with (a) as pilot.

Confirmed by user: agent IS becoming clinician-facing (so M6 judge/policy justified); PHI-off-3rd-party
is a FUTURE rule so build the provider SEAM now but keep Anthropic the only live backend.

Agent is hardcoded to Anthropic today (`import anthropic`, MODEL="claude-sonnet-4-5", no provider seam).
Multi-turn already works in `interactive_mode` REPL (grows `messages`); single-shot `--query` does not persist.

# Phase 5 Handoff — Agent Platform Hardening (fhir-agent)

> Paste this whole document as the first message of a fresh Claude Code session to
> bootstrap Phase 5. It captures brainstorming already done; **decisions marked ✅ are
> settled — implement them, don't re-open them.** Items marked 🟡 are for you to resolve
> with me early.

## 0. How to use this doc
You are resuming a multi-session effort on the `fhir-agent` project. Phases 1–4 are built
and merged. This document defines **Phase 5: Agent Platform Hardening**. Start by reading
`CLAUDE.md`, `docs/README.md`, and the memory file `phase5-agent-hardening.md`, then confirm
the 🟡 open questions in §8 with me before writing milestone docs.

## 1. Project orientation (what fhir-agent is)
An agentic healthcare platform. A clinician asks a natural-language question; an LLM/agent
layer fetches FHIR data and returns a structured recommendation. Deterministic services
decide; the agent orchestrates and explains. Two guiding sentences the whole codebase obeys:
- **AI explains and orchestrates; deterministic services decide.**
- **The legacy core is wrapped, not rewritten.**

Relevant components:
- `mcp-agent/` (Python) — **Phase 1** refill-risk-triage agent. Anthropic tool-use CLI. This
  is the **pilot target** for Phase 5 (it already has the conversational shape).
- `claims-agent/` (Python) — **Phase 2** explanation agent; explains adjudication decisions,
  non-authoritative. The **second target**, later.
- `claims-service/`, `rxclaim-emulator/`, `triage-service/`, `fhir-service/`, `epic-emulator/`,
  gateway (Kong) — the deterministic tiers the agents call.
- Docs live in `docs/` (guides) and `docs/phase2../phase4/` (per-phase). Decisions index:
  `docs/phase2/decisions.md`.

Working rules (from `CLAUDE.md`): two git worktrees; **never commit to `main`** — always a
feature branch + PR; never self-merge. Treat claims/clinical data as **PHI**.

## 2. What Phase 5 is
Harden the **agent tier** to the same standard as the decision tier, and turn the pilot agent
into a **clinician-facing conversational surface**. Built as a **shared, reusable platform
layer** (like `client/clinical` is shared) and **applied to one agent first**.

**Scope decision (✅):** Option (c) — build the platform once, **pilot on `mcp-agent`** (Phase 1
refill agent), then carry to the Phase 2 claims stack. **Explicitly defer Phase 3/4 agents.**
This is a **new phase, not an extension of Phase 2.** (Rationale in §7.)

## 3. The five topics this phase covers
1. **Memory** — short-term (the in-context transcript) vs long-term (cross-session store).
   Three distinct axes, do not conflate: per-conversation token budget (cap + compact),
   concurrent-session count (the thing that actually autoscales = compute), cross-session
   persistence store. `MAX_TOKENS=1024` today is the **output** cap, not memory. **Clinical
   rule: re-fetch from FHIR, never act on recalled state** (data changes; stale recall = the
   fail-open bug in disguise).
2. **Deployment + observability tie-in** — bounded queue + per-request deadline (avoid the
   "queue of doom"); the "queue" is really a **client-side token-bucket / concurrency limiter
   in front of the rate-limited, paid LLM API** (that, not local CPU/RAM, is the bottleneck);
   rate/cost **alerts, not auto-shed** (clinical — never silently drop a care request);
   Grafana needs a metrics pipeline **first** (instrument → Prometheus → dashboard).
3. **Observability (full)** — OTel. **A trace = one agent run; spans = reasoning steps** (each
   model call, each tool call). Use OTel `gen_ai.*` semantic conventions. **Propagate the
   traceID *through* tool calls into claims/triage/fhir** so one trace spans cognition →
   deterministic services. **PHI-redact span attributes** (that's where PHI leaks).
4. **Follow-ups + multi-model** — Meta's model = **Llama**; also **DeepSeek** (V3 general, R1
   reasoning). Self-host via vLLM/TGI/Ollama, all OpenAI-compatible. **Driver = PHI residency
   (future rule), NOT cost.** Multi-turn already works in the REPL; the hard part of multi-model
   is normalizing tool-calling + translating conversation history across providers.
5. **Output safety** — `policy.md` of NL rules loaded into the system prompt (**NOT RAG** — the
   rules always apply). RAG only for a real **knowledge base** (separate concern). **Limit the
   final answer to N enum options** via tool-with-enum-output **+** code validation **+**
   **fail-closed to REVIEW** if the model returns anything else. Optional **LLM-as-judge** on
   "important" responses for *soft* qualities only (groundedness, tone, PHI leak) — **code
   enforces hard invariants, never a judge model.** A narrow output surface is also the
   strongest control against "answers the LLM shouldn't give."

## 4. Milestones (✅ order is by dependency, not by topic number)
| M | Milestone | Topic | Why here | Weight |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **M1** | Output contract & enum gate (tool-with-enum-output; validate in code; fail-closed to REVIEW; narrow the surface) | 5 | Cheap, independent, highest safety value; extends the fail-closed thesis. Do first. | S |
| **M2** | Observability foundation (OTel traces/spans; `gen_ai.*`; traceID propagated into services; PHI redaction) | 3 | The lens. Underpins tuning M3, seeing M4, evaluating M6. | M |
| **M3** | Context & memory mgmt (explicit token budget + documented rationale; compaction at threshold; externalized session store; re-fetch-don't-recall) | 1, 4 | Needs M2's token metrics to set limits honestly. | M |
| **M4** | Deploy resilience & cost control (bounded queue + deadline; token-bucket/concurrency limiter; rate/cost alerts; Grafana dashboards) | 2 | Needs M2 metrics + M3 session model. | M |
| **M5** | Provider abstraction + cross-model follow-ups (2 adapters: Anthropic native + OpenAI-compatible; history translation) | 4 | Backbone for M6; capture follow-up code detail here for the report. | L |
| **M6** | Policy + knowledge + judge (`policy.md` into system prompt; optional RAG knowledge base; LLM-as-judge on important responses) | 5 | Sits on M1 + M5; heaviest; justified because the agent is clinician-facing. | L |

**Minimal viable cut:** M1 + M2 (closes the biggest agent-tier safety gap and gives you eyes).

## 5. Key technical decisions (✅ settled)
- **Provider layer = exactly two adapters:** `Anthropic` (native tool-use) and
  `OpenAI-compatible` (one adapter covering Llama, DeepSeek, Ollama, vLLM, and hosted
  endpoints like DeepSeek API / OpenRouter / Together / Groq). Llama vs DeepSeek = base-URL +
  model-name **config**, not new code. **Anthropic stays the only live backend for now**; the
  others exist to prove the seam.
- **Enum gate:** structured output (tool with enum) constrains *shape*; **still validate in
  code**; **fail closed to REVIEW** on anything off-contract. This is the project's fail-closed
  safety thesis applied to the agent's *output*.
- **Rules vs knowledge:** behavioral rules → `policy.md` into the system prompt (always apply,
  no retrieval). Knowledge base → RAG (retrieve relevant subset). **Do not use RAG for rules.**
- **Judge:** reserve for "important" responses; checks soft qualities; never the enforcer of
  anything code can enforce.
- **Cheap multi-model testing:** stub OpenAI-compatible server ($0 CI, same JDK-HttpServer /
  Python-http stub pattern already used in `HttpTriageClientTest`) · Ollama local ($0, weak —
  a *good adversary* for the enum gate) · hosted OpenAI-compatible (pennies, real quality).

## 6. Current code facts (verify before relying — memory may be stale)
- `mcp-agent/src/agent/agent.py`: hardcoded to Anthropic (`import anthropic`,
  `MODEL="claude-sonnet-4-5"`, `MAX_TOKENS=1024`), a `SYSTEM_PROMPT` constant, an agent loop
  `run_query(client, user_input, messages) -> (final_text, messages)`, and an
  `interactive_mode` REPL that **persists `messages` across turns** (follow-ups work in the
  REPL). The single-shot `--query` path does **not** persist across invocations.
- `mcp-agent/src/agent/tools.py`: tool definitions + `execute_tool`.
- **No observability anywhere** (no OTel/metrics/tracing) — clean slate.
- `claims-agent` has a `--no-llm` deterministic mode — useful as a live oracle for drift
  detection.

## 7. Why its own phase, not folded into Phase 2 (✅ — do not re-open)
- "Phase 2 is more cloud-ready" is **false per our own docs** — Phase 2 has cloud *design* but
  **no root Terraform module / not deployable** (the documented cloud-delivery gap).
- Cloud-readiness is **irrelevant** — all of this is built and tested locally, cloud-agnostic.
- The clinician conversational surface described (patient/med disambiguation, dispense/review/
  hold) is **Phase 1's `mcp-agent`**, not Phase 2's claims *explainer*.
- Reopening a completed, tagged, "done" Phase 2 repeats a status-truthfulness problem.
- These are **shared-platform capabilities** — build once, reuse across agents.
- Honest carve-out: the **observability slice may legitimately close Phase 2's unbuilt R15**,
  but do it *from the shared layer*, not by reopening Phase 2's M0–M7.

## 8. Open questions to resolve with the user first (🟡)
1. Exact **enum set** for the pilot surface and how REVIEW is the fail-closed sink.
2. Definition of an **"important" response** that triggers the judge.
3. **Session-store tech** (Redis vs Postgres) and **where the shared layer lives**
   (`agent-platform/` package vs in-place refactor).
4. **Memory token-budget numbers** — deliberately deferred until M2 metrics exist.
5. **Conversational transport** — CLI REPL today; web/chat UI or API? (drives streaming +
   session design).
6. **M6 RAG corpus** scope, or defer RAG.
7. **Phase number/name** confirmation (a `docs/phase5/` readiness-assessment already exists).

## 9. Cross-cutting principles (apply to every milestone)
- **Fail-closed everywhere, consistently** (enum → REVIEW; queue deadline → fail closed; judge
  disagreement → hold for human; memory → re-fetch not recall).
- **Deterministic code decides; the LLM orchestrates and explains** — the project thesis; the
  enum gate *is* this thesis applied to agent output.
- **PHI-safe is a driver, not just a constraint** (redact spans; don't persist raw PHI;
  self-hosting is a PHI *win*, which is why it's on the roadmap at all).
- **Observability first** — you can't tune memory, see deployment issues, or evaluate
  multi-model quality without M2.
- **The agent is non-authoritative** — it never decides anything clinical/financial.

## 10. Relevant existing memories to check
- `llm-tool-schema-oneof-unreliable` — **directly relevant to M1 and M5**: live Claude
  stringifies `oneOf`-typed nested tool params instead of emitting a native object. Flatten
  tool schemas; validate cross-field rules downstream. Expect worse behavior from small
  self-hosted models — another reason the enum gate validates in code.
- `pytest-test-filename-collision` — same-named `test_*.py` in different packages collide under
  this repo's `import-mode=importlib`. Check before adding any test file.
- `secret-values-never-print` — never echo secret values; redact in output. Extends naturally
  to PHI redaction in traces/logs.

## 11. A comprehensive report is owed (do not forget)
After the milestones (or several) land, the user will ask for a **comprehensive report**. It
must include, at minimum:
- **Follow-ups down to code snippets** — the `run_query(messages)→messages` mechanics, REPL
  persistence, the single-shot gap, and how each enhancement (session store, context
  compaction, tool-result compaction, re-fetch-don't-recall) changes specific lines; plus how
  the provider adapter translates conversation history for Llama/DeepSeek.
- **Memory sizing** — where each limit is set, the rationale for each number, and the autoscale
  path (per-conversation compaction vs session-count scaling vs store).
- **Observability** — the actual Grafana panels and the end-to-end trace/span/attribute schema.
Produce it *after* implementation, grounded in real code and real metrics — not predicted.

## 12. Suggested first move for Phase 5 session
Confirm the §8 open questions with the user, then draft `docs/phase5/plan.md` +
`docs/phase5/README.md` (canonical status, milestone table, decisions) on a `docs/phase5-*`
branch — planning only, no implementation — and open a docs PR. Then start **M1 (enum gate)**
as the first implementation PR, since it's cheap, independent, and the highest safety value.

  layer lives (new `agent-platform/` package vs in-place refactor).

  data, not guessed.

  (drives streaming + session design).

management exists today.

`docs/phase5/` holds only a readiness-assessment; branch `docs/phase5-readiness-assessment`).
A full **handoff document** (title "Phase 5 Handoff — Agent Platform Hardening") was pasted into
session and is the canonical source for scope, milestones §4, decisions §5, code facts §6, open
questions §8, cross-cutting principles §9, and the report spec §11 — treat that doc's content as
settled/authoritative over any summary here if they ever conflict.

## The 5 topics (fixed numbering, referenced throughout by number)

1. **Memory** — token budget/compaction, session-count autoscale, cross-session store,
   re-fetch-don't-recall.
2. **Deployment + observability tie-in** — bounded queue/deadline, token-bucket/concurrency
   limiter in front of the paid LLM API, rate/cost alerts (not auto-shed), Grafana dashboards.
3. **Observability (full)** — OTel: trace=one agent run, spans=reasoning steps, `gen_ai.*`
   attributes, traceID propagated into claims/triage/fhir, PHI-redacted span attributes.
4. **Follow-ups + multi-model** — provider abstraction (Anthropic native + OpenAI-compatible),
   Llama/DeepSeek as config not code, conversation-history translation across providers.
5. **Output safety** — policy.md into system prompt (NOT RAG), tool-with-enum-output + code
   validation + fail-closed to REVIEW, LLM-as-judge on "important" responses for soft qualities
   only (code enforces hard invariants).

## Decided (✅ per handoff doc — do not re-open)

- Phase 5 is its OWN phase, NOT folded into Phase 2 (see [[cloud-delivery-gap]]; rationale in
  handoff §7).
- Strategy: build the platform once as a shared reusable layer, **pilot on `mcp-agent`** (Phase 1
  refill-triage agent), then carry to Phase 2's claims stack. Phase 3/4 agents explicitly deferred.
- Agent is becoming clinician-facing → M6 (policy+judge) is justified.
- PHI-off-third-party = a FUTURE rule → build the provider seam now, **Anthropic stays the only
  live backend**. Target providers when activated: Anthropic + Llama + DeepSeek.
- Provider abstraction = exactly **two adapters**: Anthropic (native) + OpenAI-compatible (covers
  Llama, DeepSeek, Ollama, vLLM, hosted endpoints). Model choice becomes config, not code.
- Output safety is a MUST: enum-gate + code validation + fail-closed to REVIEW.
- Rules → policy.md in system prompt; RAG reserved only for a genuine knowledge base.
- Milestone order (dependency, not topic-number order): **M1 enum-gate (topic 5) → M2 OTel
  foundation (topic 3) → M3 memory/context+session store (topics 1,4) → M4 deploy resilience+cost
  alerts (topic 2) → M5 provider abstraction (topic 4) → M6 policy+knowledge+judge (topic 5).**
  Minimal viable cut = M1 + M2.
- Cheap Llama/DeepSeek testing: stub OpenAI-compatible server ($0 CI) / Ollama local ($0, weak
  adversary for enum gate) / hosted OpenAI-compatible — DeepSeek API/OpenRouter/Groq (pennies).

## Open issues (🟡 handoff §8 — resolve with user before milestone docs)

1. Exact enum set for the pilot surface + how REVIEW is the fail-closed sink.
2. Definition of an "important" response that triggers the judge.
3. Session-store tech (Redis vs Postgres) and where the shared layer lives (`agent-platform/`
   package vs in-place refactor).
4. Memory token-budget numbers — deferred until M2 metrics exist.
5. Conversational transport — CLI REPL today; web/chat UI or API? (drives streaming/session design).
6. M6 RAG corpus scope, or defer RAG.
7. Phase number/name confirmation; whether the observability slice formally closes Phase 2's
   unbuilt R15.

## Comprehensive report obligation (handoff §11 — owed after milestones land, not before)

Must include, mapped to topic numbers above:
- **Topic 4** down to code snippets: `run_query(messages)→messages` mechanics, REPL persistence,
  the single-shot `--query` gap, and how each enhancement (session store, context compaction,
  tool-result compaction, re-fetch-don't-recall) changes specific lines; plus how the provider
  adapter translates conversation history for Llama/DeepSeek.
- **Topic 1**: where each memory limit is set, the rationale for each number, and the autoscale
  path (per-conversation compaction vs session-count scaling vs persistence store).
- **Topics 2 & 3**: the actual Grafana panels and the end-to-end trace/span/attribute schema.
Must be grounded in real code and real metrics after implementation — not predicted.

## Current code facts (handoff §6 — verify before relying, may drift)

`mcp-agent/src/agent/agent.py`: hardcoded to Anthropic (`import anthropic`,
`MODEL="claude-sonnet-4-5"`, `MAX_TOKENS=1024` — this is the OUTPUT cap, not memory), a
`SYSTEM_PROMPT` constant, `run_query(client, user_input, messages) -> (final_text, messages)`,
and `interactive_mode` REPL that persists `messages` across turns (follow-ups work in REPL;
single-shot `--query` does not persist). `mcp-agent/src/agent/tools.py` holds tool defs +
`execute_tool`. No observability anywhere yet — clean slate. `claims-agent` has a `--no-llm`
deterministic mode usable as a live oracle for drift detection.

## Related memories flagged as relevant (handoff §10)

[[llm-tool-schema-oneof-unreliable]] — directly relevant to M1 and M5 (flatten tool schemas,
validate cross-field rules downstream; expect worse behavior from small self-hosted models).
[[pytest-test-filename-collision]] — check before adding any new test file.
[[secret-values-never-print]] — extends naturally to PHI redaction in traces/logs (topic 3).

## Suggested first move (handoff §12)

Confirm §8 open questions with user → draft `docs/phase5/plan.md` + `docs/phase5/README.md` on a
`docs/phase5-*` branch (planning only) → open docs PR → then start M1 (enum gate) as first
implementation PR.

# mcp-agent Investigation Report

Full file inventory (`mcp-agent/`): `pyproject.toml`, `README.md`, `Dockerfile`, `src/agent/__init__.py` (empty), `src/agent/agent.py` (269 lines), `src/agent/tools.py` (236 lines), `src/agent/format.py` (90 lines), `tests/__init__.py` (empty), `tests/test_e2e_demo_flow.py` (304 lines). That is the entire package — no `conftest.py`, no config file, no logging module, no observability module, no session-storage module.

## 1. Verification of handoff claims

- **`import anthropic`, `MODEL="claude-sonnet-4-5"`, `MAX_TOKENS=1024`** — CONFIRMED, `mcp-agent/src/agent/agent.py:33,47-48`:
  ```
  33  import anthropic
  ...
  47  MODEL = "claude-sonnet-4-5"
  48  MAX_TOKENS = 1024
  ```

- **`SYSTEM_PROMPT` constant** — CONFIRMED, `agent.py:50-65`, a multi-line string defining the clinical-assistant persona (mandates calling `get_patient_summary` before `assess_refill_risk`, mandates including risk level/rationale/RiskAssessment ID/recommendation, instructs to be "direct and emphatic" on HIGH risk, and "never fabricate patient data").

- **`run_query(client, user_input, messages) -> (final_text, messages)`** — CONFIRMED, `agent.py:72-139`. Actual signature is `run_query(client, user_input, messages=None, verbose=True) -> tuple[str, list[dict]]`, so the handoff's description is accurate but incomplete — it omits the `verbose` parameter. It loops on `response.stop_reason == "tool_use"`, calling `execute_tool` for every tool_use block and feeding results back, until a non-tool_use response, then returns `(final_text, messages)`.

- **`interactive_mode` REPL persists `messages`; `--query` does NOT persist** — CONFIRMED.
  - `interactive_mode` (`agent.py:205-231`): initializes `messages: list[dict] = []` once outside the `while True:` loop (line 208) and reassigns it each turn via `final_text, messages = run_query(client, user_input, messages)` (line 225) — so conversation state persists across REPL turns.
  - `non_interactive_mode` (`agent.py:234-246`): calls `run_query(client, query)` with no `messages` argument (line 238), and the process exits after one query (`main()` → `sys.exit(non_interactive_mode(...))`, lines 262-263). Each `--query` invocation is a fresh process with empty history — confirmed no persistence across invocations (and there's no on-disk session store to persist to — see item 5).

- **`tools.py` holds tool definitions + `execute_tool`** — CONFIRMED. `TOOL_DEFINITIONS` list at `tools.py:29-81`, dispatcher `execute_tool(name, inputs) -> str` at `tools.py:221-236`.

- **No observability (no OTel/metrics/tracing) anywhere in mcp-agent** — CONFIRMED. Grep for `opentelemetry|otel|prometheus|statsd|datadog|jaeger|tracing|metrics|logging.getLogger|logger =|structlog` across `mcp-agent/` returned zero hits. The only "instrumentation" is `print()`-based console output for tool calls/results (`_print_tool_call`/`_print_tool_result`, `agent.py:142-175`) and formatted terminal strings in `format.py` — purely for interactive/demo display, not logs or metrics.

## 2. Tool schemas

Two tools, both defined in `mcp-agent/src/agent/tools.py:29-81`:

1. **`get_patient_summary`** (`tools.py:31-49`)
   - `input_schema.properties`: `name` (string, required) — "Patient name or partial name to search for."
   - `required: ["name"]`
   - Flat, single string param. No nesting.

2. **`assess_refill_risk`** (`tools.py:50-80`)
   - `input_schema.properties`: `patient_id` (string, required), `medication_id` (string, optional)
   - `required: ["patient_id"]`
   - Flat, two string params. No nesting.

**No `oneOf`, `anyOf`, `allOf`, nested objects, arrays, or enum types appear anywhere in the tool `input_schema`s.** Both schemas are as simple/robust as JSON-schema for tool-calling gets — flat objects with only string properties. This is a mitigating fact, not a risk, for any "fragile schema" critique in the handoff — there's nothing schema-fragile here to harden.

**Enum-typed *output* fields already in use (not input schemas, but worth flagging since the handoff-relevant risk area is agent output validation):**
- Risk level is an informal string enum `HIGH | MODERATE | LOW` (plus a fallback `"UNKNOWN"`) threaded through several places:
  - `tools.py:197-202` extracts `risk_code` from the triage service's FHIR `RiskAssessment.prediction[0].outcome.coding[0].code`, defaulting to the literal string `"UNKNOWN"` if any key is missing (via chained `.get(..., {})` / `.get(..., [{}])[0]` calls — fails silently to `"UNKNOWN"` rather than erroring).
  - `format.py:10-14` (`RISK_ICONS`) and `format.py:16-20` (`RISK_LABELS`) are dicts keyed on `"HIGH"/"MODERATE"/"LOW"` with `.get(risk_level, "❓")` / `.get(risk_level, f"{risk_level} RISK")` fallbacks for unrecognized values — so an unknown code degrades gracefully to a generic label rather than crashing, but there is **no schema/enum constraint enforced anywhere** (no Python `Enum`, no Pydantic model, no JSON-schema `enum` list) — it's all string comparison by convention.

## 3. Error handling / safety today

- **FHIR-service errors**: `get_patient_summary` catches `FHIRClientError` and `RuntimeError` (missing `FHIR_GATEWAY_URL`) and returns `{"error": "..."}` dicts (`tools.py:118-121`) rather than raising — these get serialized to JSON and handed back to Claude as a tool_result, so the LLM sees the error as text and must decide how to respond. No retry, no backoff, no circuit breaker.
- **Triage-service errors**: `assess_refill_risk` catches `httpx.HTTPStatusError` (extracts `detail` from the JSON error body if present) and `httpx.RequestError` (network-level failure, e.g. service down) and again returns `{"error": "..."}` dicts (`tools.py:184-194`) rather than raising. Same pattern — no retry/backoff/timeout-retry logic; there is a flat 30-second `httpx.post(..., timeout=30.0)` (`tools.py:180`) but no configurable per-call timeout, no circuit breaker.
- **Malformed/unexpected triage response shape**: the field-extraction at `tools.py:197-205` uses defensive chained `.get()` with `{}` / `[{}]` defaults, so a malformed response degrades to `risk_code = "UNKNOWN"` rather than throwing a `KeyError`/`IndexError` — this is effectively **fail-open at the parsing layer** (an unparseable/malformed response is silently treated as an "UNKNOWN" risk string handed to the LLM as ordinary text, not surfaced as an error or blocked). There is no code path that refuses to answer or forces a "cannot verify" response when the risk parsing fails this way.
- **Ambiguous patient lookups**: `get_patient_summary` distinguishes not-found (`found: False` + suggestion message, `tools.py:123-128`) from multiple-matches (`found: True, multiple_matches: True, count, patients[], message` asking for clarification, `tools.py:140-155`). This is structured data the LLM is *expected* to use to ask the clinician to disambiguate (per `SYSTEM_PROMPT`'s "if you cannot find a patient, say so clearly"), but **nothing programmatically prevents** the LLM from picking one of several matches and proceeding to call `assess_refill_risk` anyway — there's no code-level guard forcing disambiguation.
- **Top-level exception handling**: both `interactive_mode` (`agent.py:224-231`) and `non_interactive_mode` (`agent.py:237-246`) wrap `run_query` in `try/except anthropic.APIError` (prints a formatted error) and a bare `except Exception` (prints error). Notably, `interactive_mode`'s bare-`Exception` handler **re-raises after printing** (`agent.py:229-231`, `raise` on the line after the error print) — meaning an unexpected exception crashes the whole REPL process; `non_interactive_mode`'s equivalent handler does not re-raise, just returns exit code 1 (`agent.py:244-246`). This asymmetry (crash-on-exception in interactive mode, graceful-exit in `--query` mode) is worth flagging as inconsistent behavior.
- **Validation of the LLM's final answer**: **None.** `run_query` returns `final_text` built by simply concatenating every `block.text` from the model's final (non-tool-use) response content (`agent.py:130-133`), and both entry points just `print(agent_response(final_text))` (`agent.py:226,239`) with zero post-hoc validation — no check that risk level/assessment ID were actually included, no regex/schema validation of the narrative, no guard against the model contradicting the tool output or hallucinating a risk level not returned by the triage service. The `SYSTEM_PROMPT` *instructs* the model to always include patient name/risk level/rationale/assessment ID (lines 57-61) and to never fabricate data (line 65), but this is prompt-only guidance — nothing in code enforces or checks it. This is a legitimate, real gap for a "hardening" phase to target.
- **Fail-open vs fail-closed**: overall the system is **fail-open** — every error path (FHIR down, triage down, malformed response, unknown risk code) degrades to returning descriptive text/JSON that gets handed to the LLM to narrate, rather than any code path that blocks/refuses output or requires a human override. There is no mechanism that prevents the agent from producing a "dispense" recommendation in the presence of a tool/service failure — nothing hard-stops output when `{"error": ...}` payloads are seen; it's entirely up to the LLM's own judgment per the system prompt.

## 4. Tests

Single test file: `mcp-agent/tests/test_e2e_demo_flow.py` (304 lines, discovered via `pyproject.toml`'s `[tool.pytest.ini_options] testpaths = ["tests"]`).

Coverage, by class:
- `TestKristleMrazHighRisk` (`test_e2e_demo_flow.py:101-173`) — `get_patient_summary` finds Kristle; `assess_refill_risk` returns HIGH; full two-step demo flow (name → ID → risk) for the penicillin/amoxicillin conflict scenario.
- `TestJohnDoeLowRisk` (`test_e2e_demo_flow.py:180-240`) — mirror of the above for the LOW-risk, no-conflict scenario.
- `TestEdgeCases` (`test_e2e_demo_flow.py:247-304`) — patient-not-found (`found: False`), multiple-matches disambiguation, `medication_id` forwarded correctly in the triage payload, triage-service unreachable (`httpx.ConnectError` → structured `{"error": ...}`), and unknown tool name → structured error.

**What is NOT tested:** `agent.py` itself is completely untested — no test exercises `run_query`, `interactive_mode`, `non_interactive_mode`, `main()`, `_check_env`, or the Anthropic `client.messages.create` tool-use loop. All tests operate directly on `agent.tools.execute_tool` / `get_patient_summary` / `assess_refill_risk`, with the Anthropic API itself never invoked or mocked anywhere. There is no test of the CLI argument parsing, env-var validation error paths, or multi-turn REPL message persistence.

**Test-double pattern used**: `unittest.mock.patch` + `MagicMock`, patching `agent.tools._fhir_client` (to return a `MagicMock` FHIR client) and `agent.tools.httpx.post` (to return a `MagicMock` response) — see e.g. `test_e2e_demo_flow.py:110-111, 126-131`. **This is pure object-mocking, not an HTTP stub server.**

**On the "HttpTriageClientTest" stub-server pattern**: I found `HttpTriageClientTest.java` — it lives in **`claims-service/src/test/java/com/payer/claims/HttpTriageClientTest.java`**, not in `triage-service` as the handoff doc's phrasing might suggest (worth flagging: triage-service itself, at `triage-service/src/triage/`, has no HTTP-client tests of its own — it's the server, not a client of another HTTP service).   ...
  ```
  47  MODEL = "claude-sonnet-4-5"
  48  MAX_TOKENS = 1024
  ```

- **`SYSTEM_PROMPT` constant** — CONFIRMED, `agent.py:50-65`, a multi-line string defining the clinical-assistant persona (mandates calling `get_patient_summary` before `assess_refill_risk`, mandates including risk level/rationale/RiskAssessment ID/recommendation, instructs to be "direct and emphatic" on HIGH risk, and "never fabricate patient data").

- **`run_query(client, user_input, messages) -> (final_text, messages)`** — CONFIRMED, `agent.py:72-139`. Actual signature is `run_query(client, user_input, messages=None, verbose=True) -> tuple[str, list[dict]]`, so the handoff's description is accurate but incomplete — it omits the `verbose` parameter. It loops on `response.stop_reason == "tool_use"`, calling `execute_tool` for every tool_use block and feeding results back, until a non-tool_use response, then returns `(final_text, messages)`.

- **`interactive_mode` REPL persists `messages`; `--query` does NOT persist** — CONFIRMED.
  - `interactive_mode` (`agent.py:205-231`): initializes `messages: list[dict] = []` once outside the `while True:` loop (line 208) and reassigns it each turn via `final_text, messages = run_query(client, user_input, messages)` (line 225) — so conversation state persists across REPL turns.
  - `non_interactive_mode` (`agent.py:234-246`): calls `run_query(client, query)` with no `messages` argument (line 238), and the process exits after one query (`main()` → `sys.exit(non_interactive_mode(...))`, lines 262-263). - `claims-agent` has a deterministic mode; `mcp-agent` does not.
- Neither has persisted memory/session storage (both just hold `messages` in a Python list for process lifetime), and **neither has any observability/tracing instrumentation** (no OTel, no structured logging beyond print statements, in either agent).

So: no provider abstraction, no durable memory, no observability exists in *either* agent — the plan's premise that `claims-agent` might already have infrastructure `mcp-agent` lacks (or vice versa) is **not supported**; they're both minimal/equivalent in that respect except for the deterministic-mode oracle in `claims-agent`.

## 3. "Cloud-delivery-gap" claim

This is the *authoritative* decision-maker.

It wasn't there; `RateLimitMiddleware` was the only middleware that existed... The general lesson: 'Fixed here' in a design doc describes an intent until something in the codebase actually points back at it — treat a security-relevant claim with no corresponding file/line reference as unverified, not as done." **A live, currently-unfixed PHI exposure exists in the gateway today** — `docs/gateway-runbook.md:248-250`: > "**PHI in gateway logs (⚠️ applies to Phase 1 today).** Kong's `file-log` records request URIs, which contain patient and member identifiers. Treat gateway logs as **restricted**, or scrub them (R14). This is a real, current exposure — not a Phase 2 concern." This confirms Kong's `fhir-request-log` plugin (`gateway/kong/kong-plugins.yaml:127-143`) writes raw `request.uri` (e.g. `/fhir/Patient/123`) to stdout — an acknowledged, still-open PHI gap that any new agent-tier observability work should not repeat. ## 3. Gateway (Kong) rate limiting There are **two separate Kong deployments** in this repo (per `gateway/README.md` and `docs/gateway-runbook.md`), and their rate-limiting posture differs: **Phase 1 (Kubernetes/Helm KIC, deployed today, fronts only `fhir-service`)** — `gateway/kong/kong-plugins.yaml`, `fhir-rate-limit` KongPlugin: ```yaml plugin: rate-limiting config: second: 10 # max 10 requests/sec (DoS/burst protection) day: 1000 # max 1000 requests/day (usage quota) policy: cluster # counters written to Neon (kongdb) on every request hide_client_headers: false error_code: 429 error_message: "API rate limit exceeded. The plan's "alert not auto-shed" design for the LLM-call limiter would be a **new** pattern relative to every rate-limiting precedent in the repo, worth flagging explicitly as a deliberate departure, not an extension of existing convention — especially in tension with the "never silently drop a care request" framing, since "alert only" on a paid, clinical-tier API means requests still go through uncapped in practice. ## 4. Kong / infra observability — Prometheus Yes, Prometheus is already wired into the **Phase 1** Kong config. `gateway/kong/kong-plugins.yaml:99-126`, `fhir-prometheus` (`KongClusterPlugin`, global scope): ```yaml plugin: prometheus config: status_code_metrics: true latency_metrics: true bandwidth_metrics: true upstream_health_metrics: true ``` `gateway/README.md:367-386` documents the endpoint (`kong-kong-metrics:8100/metrics`) and states scraping depends on enabling GKE Managed Prometheus — the "Known Limitations" section is explicit: **"Prometheus metrics are declared but not scraped until Google Cloud Managed Prometheus is enabled in GKE. Queue / deadline / timeout / circuit-breaker patterns No circuit breaker is implemented anywhere in the deterministic tier — it is explicitly deferred. `HttpTriageClient.java:24`: **"Adding a circuit breaker here is follow-up work; it changes latency, not this policy."** (I.e., the fail-closed *policy* — UNKNOWN on any failure — already covers correctness; a circuit breaker would only be a latency/throughput optimization on top of it.) Timeout conventions found (`grep -rnE "deadline|timeout|asyncio\.wait_for|circuit.?breaker|Queue\(" triage-service claims-service fhir-service gateway`): - **`claims-service` → `triage-service` HTTP call** (`HttpTriageClient.java:32-34,50-51`): `connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5))` at the `HttpClient` level, plus a per-request `timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(20))`. Both a connect-phase and an overall-request deadline are set explicitly, and — critically — a timeout is caught by the same `catch (Exception e)` block that maps to `RiskLevel.UNKNOWN` (line 76-79), so a timeout is treated identically to any other transport failure under the fail-closed policy, not as a special "assume safe" case. - **`claims-service` → `fhir-service`** (`HapiFhirClient.java:25`): `ctx.getRestfulClientFactory().setSocketTimeout(20_000)` — same 20s order of magnitude. - **`fhir-service` (HAPI/Spring config)**: `application.yaml:227-228` / `application-cds.yaml:207-208`: `timeoutSeconds: 30`, `socketTimeout: 60` (for outbound calls HAPI itself makes, e.g. CDS Hooks/terminology); `application-neon.yaml:66-67`: DB pool `connection-timeout: 30000`, `idle-timeout: 600000`. - **Kong**: no explicit request-level timeout override found in the DB-less `kong.tmpl.yml`/`kong-plugins.yaml`/`kong-ingress.yaml` beyond Kong's own defaults; `kong-ingress.yaml:55-56` notes the old `proxy` (timeouts) field is deprecated in KIC v3+ and timeouts are now expected to live in the k8s Service annotations on `fhir-service/k8s/service.yaml` instead. - No `Queue`, `asyncio.wait_for`, or any queuing/backpressure primitive appears anywhere in `triage-service`, `claims-service`, or `fhir-service` — the Python `triage-service` is fully synchronous FastAPI with no explicit per-request timeout of its own (it relies on the *caller's* client-side timeout, i.e., `claims-service`'s 20s, to bound the interaction — there's no server-side deadline enforcement in `triage-service` itself). **Convention for the agent tier to match:** every existing cross-service call sets an explicit connect timeout distinct from an explicit overall-request timeout (5s/20s pattern), and treats a timeout as a first-class member of the *same* failure-handling branch as any other unrecoverable error (mapping straight to the fail-closed `UNKNOWN`/PEND outcome) — it is not a special "maybe retry, maybe assume okay" path. A circuit breaker is explicitly out of scope by design precedent ("follow-up work; it changes latency, not this policy") — so if the Phase 5 plan wants a circuit breaker in front of the LLM API, it should note this diverges from the stated repo precedent (timeouts + fail-closed mapping, no breaker) rather than presenting a breaker as consistent with existing practice.

This is **fail-closed / block-over-limit**: exceeding either window returns HTTP `429` with `Retry-After`/`X-RateLimit-*` headers — no degrade mode, no silent shedding. **Phase 2 (DB-less docker-compose Kong, the "canonical Phase 2 gateway," fronts `/claims`, `/fhir`, `/triage`)** — `gateway/kong/kong.tmpl.yml`: only a `key-auth` plugin is configured. **No rate-limiting plugin exists on the Phase 2 gateway at all** — this is the gateway that fronts `triage-service` and `claims-service` locally/in the docker-compose topology. So today, rate limiting is scoped only to `fhir-service` via the older Phase 1 KIC deployment; `triage-service` and `claims-service` have no gateway-level rate limit. Consumer provisioning already anticipates an agent consumer: `gateway/README.md:405-411` lists suggested consumers including `mcp-agent` — "LLM orchestration layer" — but no rate-limit plugin is attached to it specifically anywhere in the repo. **A second, independent, in-process rate-limiting precedent exists** (not gateway-based) — `provider-registry-service/src/provider_registry/ratelimit.py`, `RateLimitMiddleware`: a sliding-window (deque-based, not token-bucket) per-caller-IP limiter, explicitly "defense-in-depth against a compromised/buggy internal caller," in-memory (resets per instance, doesn't coordinate across replicas — an accepted limitation). It is also fail-closed/block-over-limit: ```python if len(hits) >= self._max_requests: return JSONResponse(status_code=429, content={"error_type": "rate_limited", "message": "too many requests"}) ``` This is the closest existing analog to the plan's proposed client-side token-bucket: an application-level (not gateway) rate limiter that hard-rejects (429) rather than degrading — but note it's a sliding-window counter, not a token bucket, and every existing rate limiter in this repo (gateway and in-process) **blocks/rejects over limit**; none of them "alert but don't shed." The plan's "alert not auto-shed" design for the LLM-call limiter would be a **new** pattern relative to every rate-limiting precedent in the repo, worth flagging explicitly as a deliberate departure, not an extension of existing convention — especially in tension with the "never silently drop a care request" framing, since "alert only" on a paid, clinical-tier API means requests still go through uncapped in practice. ## 4. Kong / infra observability — Prometheus Yes, Prometheus is already wired into the **Phase 1** Kong config. `gateway/kong/kong-plugins.yaml:99-126`, `fhir-prometheus` (`KongClusterPlugin`, global scope): ```yaml plugin: prometheus config: status_code_metrics: true latency_metrics: true bandwidth_metrics: true upstream_health_metrics: true ``` `gateway/README.md:367-386` documents the endpoint (`kong-kong-metrics:8100/metrics`) and states scraping depends on enabling GKE Managed Prometheus — the "Known Limitations" section is explicit: **"Prometheus metrics are declared but not scraped until Google Cloud Managed Prometheus is enabled in GKE. The `/metrics` endpoint works immediately for manual inspection."** So Prometheus export exists and is documented but is not confirmed as actively scraped in the deployed environment. Also note: this Prometheus plugin is only declared in the **Phase 1** KIC config (`kong-plugins.yaml`) — the Phase 2 docker-compose `kong.tmpl.yml` used locally for `triage`/`claims`/`fhir` has no Prometheus (or any metrics) plugin configured at all. `docs/phase2/requirements.md` R15 separately commits to "Metrics via Micrometer/Prometheus (Java) and Prometheus (Python) → Google Managed Prometheus (already declared in `kong-values.yaml`)" — i.e., the Phase 2 plan text references the Phase 1 Kong Prometheus declaration as the shared observability backend, but I found no Phase-2-service-level (triage/claims/fhir app-level, non-Kong) Prometheus exporter code in this pass — worth double-checking against another agent's findings if one specifically searched app-level `/metrics` endpoints in `triage-service`/`claims-service`. ## 5. fhir-service / claims-service error-shape conventions The commit log confirms the "three quirks" reference: `ceffc27 feat(phase4 M4): the three quirks -- pagination, required params, error shape` (in `epic-emulator`, not fhir-service/claims-service directly) — quirk **C** is "Error shape," implemented by `EpicOperationOutcome` (`epic-emulator/README.md:113-116`): > "**C — Error shape.** `EpicOperationOutcome` builds the `OperationOutcome` body used by quirk B's rejection and by the auth gate's `401` (upgraded from M2's plain JSON). Deliberately **not** applied to `TokenController`'s own OAuth2 token-endpoint errors — different protocol layer, different standard shape (decision E14)." **Across the repo there are actually three different, unreconciled error-shape conventions**, not one unified pattern: 1. **FHIR `OperationOutcome`** (HL7 standard shape: `issue[].severity` / `issue[].code` / `issue[].diagnostics`, `application/fhir+json`) — used by `claims-service`'s `ClaimValidationAdvice.java` for malformed-claim rejection (400) and by `epic-emulator`'s `EpicOperationOutcome` for its quirks. `ClaimValidationAdvice.java` docstring: distinguishes a **denial** (a decision about a valid claim, belongs in the audit trail) from a **malformed request** (not a claim at all, "must leave no trace") — deliberately not persisted/audited the same way. Field-level violations are explicitly sorted `(field, message)` for determinism, echoed as `OperationOutcome.issue[].diagnostics`; unparseable bodies get a generic message with no payload echo, "since claims are treated as PHI (R14)." `fhir-service` (HAPI FHIR JPA server) also returns `OperationOutcome` by default for its own errors (standard HAPI behavior). 2. **FastAPI default `{"detail": "..."}`** — `triage-service/src/triage/main.py` uses plain `HTTPException(status_code=..., detail=...)` (404 patient/medication not found, 502 FHIR error) with no structured error-type field. 3. **A custom structured JSON shape** — `provider-registry-service/src/provider_registry/errors.py`: `{"error_type": ..., "message": ...}` (optionally `field`), with dedicated FastAPI exception handlers per error class (`not_found` → 404, `upstream_unavailable` → 503, plus a validation handler and a DB-operational handler) — this is the repo's "three error-taxonomy classes" referenced in `docs/testing-guide.md:141`. **Implication for the agent tier:** there is no single existing error-shape standard to mirror. FHIR-surface-facing services (claims-service, epic-emulator, fhir-service) converge on `OperationOutcome`; the two internal Python microservices diverge from each other (plain `detail` string vs. structured `error_type`/`message`). A fail-closed agent-tier REVIEW outcome should pick deliberately — e.g., mirror `OperationOutcome` if it's meant to be FHIR-audit-storable (like triage's own `RiskAssessment` response), or mirror `provider-registry-service`'s `{error_type, message}` taxonomy if it's an internal-API-only concern — and should document that choice, since the repo itself doesn't have one converged convention to inherit implicitly. ## 6. Queue / deadline / timeout / circuit-breaker patterns No circuit breaker is implemented anywhere in the deterministic tier — it is explicitly deferred. `HttpTriageClient.java:24`: **"Adding a circuit breaker here is follow-up work; it changes latency, not this policy."** (I.e., the fail-closed *policy* — UNKNOWN on any failure — already covers correctness; a circuit breaker would only be a latency/throughput optimization on top of it.) Timeout conventions found (`grep -rnE "deadline|timeout|asyncio\.wait_for|circuit.?breaker|Queue\(" triage-service claims-service fhir-service gateway`): - **`claims-service` → `triage-service` HTTP call** (`HttpTriageClient.java:32-34,50-51`): `connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5))` at the `HttpClient` level, plus a per-request `timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(20))`. Both a connect-phase and an overall-request deadline are set explicitly, and — critically — a timeout is caught by the same `catch (Exception e)` block that maps to `RiskLevel.UNKNOWN` (line 76-79), so a timeout is treated identically to any other transport failure under the fail-closed policy, not as a special "assume safe" case. - **`claims-service` → `fhir-service`** (`HapiFhirClient.java:25`): `ctx.getRestfulClientFactory().setSocketTimeout(20_000)` — same 20s order of magnitude. - **`fhir-service` (HAPI/Spring config)**: `application.yaml:227-228` / `application-cds.yaml:207-208`: `timeoutSeconds: 30`, `socketTimeout: 60` (for outbound calls HAPI itself makes, e.g. CDS Hooks/terminology); `application-neon.yaml:66-67`: DB pool `connection-timeout: 30000`, `idle-timeout: 600000`. - **Kong**: no explicit request-level timeout override found in the DB-less `kong.tmpl.yml`/`kong-plugins.yaml`/`kong-ingress.yaml` beyond Kong's own defaults; `kong-ingress.yaml:55-56` notes the old `proxy` (timeouts) field is deprecated in KIC v3+ and timeouts are now expected to live in the k8s Service annotations on `fhir-service/k8s/service.yaml` instead. - No `Queue`, `asyncio.wait_for`, or any queuing/backpressure primitive appears anywhere in `triage-service`, `claims-service`, or `fhir-service` — the Python `triage-service` is fully synchronous FastAPI with no explicit per-request timeout of its own (it relies on the *caller's* client-side timeout, i.e., `claims-service`'s 20s, to bound the interaction — there's no server-side deadline enforcement in `triage-service` itself). **Convention for the agent tier to match:** every existing cross-service call sets an explicit connect timeout distinct from an explicit overall-request timeout (5s/20s pattern), and treats a timeout as a first-class member of the *same* failure-handling branch as any other unrecoverable error (mapping straight to the fail-closed `UNKNOWN`/PEND outcome) — it is not a special "maybe retry, maybe assume okay" path. A circuit breaker is explicitly out of scope by design precedent ("follow-up work; it changes latency, not this policy") — so if the Phase 5 plan wants a circuit breaker in front of the LLM API, it should note this diverges from the stated repo precedent (timeouts + fail-closed mapping, no breaker) rather than presenting a breaker as consistent with existing practice.

# Phase 5 Critique — findings from the actual codebase and docs

Four parallel audits (mcp-agent code, claims-agent/Phase 2, Phase 4/Phase 5 docs + observability infra, deterministic-tier conventions). No planning below — just what's confirmed, what's wrong, and what needs a decision from you before any milestone doc gets written.

## What's clear and holds up

**The handoff doc's code claims about mcp-agent are all accurate.** `agent.py`'s hardcoded Anthropic client/model/token cap, `SYSTEM_PROMPT`, `run_query(messages)→messages` mechanics, REPL persistence vs. `--query` non-persistence, `tools.py`'s two tools — all verified line-for-line. Good foundation to build the report on later.

**The cloud-delivery-gap claim is accurate and well-documented**, quotable directly from `docs/phase2/plan.md`'s "⚠️ Cloud-delivery gap" callout and `decisions.md` D8: no root Terraform module, no `deploy-phase2.sh`, only per-service Cloud Run stubs. The "Phase 2 isn't more cloud-ready" reasoning is sound.

**The status-truthfulness incident is real**, commit `0fcc196` ("status truth, safety semantics, gateway runbook, ADR index") — a reviewer did catch Phase 2 asserting things the repo didn't support. That precedent is legitimate grounds for not casually reopening Phase 2.

**A fail-closed convention already exists and is load-bearing** in `claims-service`: `Severity{DENY,PEND,REVIEW,INFO}` / `Outcome{APPROVED,DENIED,PENDED,ROUTED_FOR_REVIEW}`, plus the documented "unknown ≠ safe" lesson (`docs/testing-guide.md`: *"Make 'I don't know' a distinct value"*). `REVIEW` is already a specific, defined status in this codebase, not a blank slate — the plan's "fail-closed to REVIEW" choice happens to align with it.

## Corrections needed

- **Phase 2 was never "tagged."** Only `phase1-v1` exists as a git tag. Phase 2's "done" status lives in prose (`docs/phase2/README.md`'s canonical statement), not a tag. If this word carries into a milestone doc, it repeats an error.
- **`HttpTriageClientTest`'s stub-server pattern lives in `claims-service` (Java), not `triage-service`.** Triage-service has no HTTP-client tests of its own (it's the server, not a client). Reusing that pattern for mcp-agent means porting a Java/JUnit idiom to Python — nothing equivalent exists in Python yet, and no stub-server library (`respx`, etc.) is a dependency anywhere.
- **The R15 ("OTel tracing wired") claim in Phase 2's own milestone table is itself inflated.** No `opentelemetry` or `micrometer` dependency exists in `claims-service`/`rxclaim-emulator`, no `traceId`/correlation-ID code anywhere. This is a second, uncaught instance of the same documentation-vs-code gap the reviewer flagged once already — worth deciding whether to fix in Phase 2's docs opportunistically or just note it and move on.

## The collision that needs your call first

**`docs/phase5/` already has content, and it isn't this.** The only file there — `phase4-testing-and-analysis.md`, on this exact branch — is explicitly labeled *"DRAFT... not a Phase 5 PRD itself,"* and its entire content is a post-merge Phase 4 safety review, headlined by a **live, unfixed clinical-safety bug**: `epic-emulator`'s 20-record pagination cap silently drops allergy records, flipping a HIGH-risk (do-not-dispense) conflict to LOW-risk (safe to dispense) when a patient has >20 allergies. The doc says this should be fixed "**before Phase 5 starts**," and separately proposes Phase 5 scope around decomposing `epic-emulator`, not agent hardening.

`docs/phase4/README.md` and `docs/README.md` both currently reserve "Phase 5" for that epic-emulator decomposition work — "no timeline set," but the slot isn't empty. Nothing in the roadmap reserves "Phase 6" either. So: is agent-platform-hardening now Phase 5 (superseding/absorbing the epic-emulator content) or a different phase number, and — separately from naming — does the open pagination bug need to be dealt with before or alongside this work, given it's a live false-negative on the exact drug-allergy-conflict check `mcp-agent` calls?

## Things the plan should align to rather than invent

- **The triage rule engine (`rules.py`) is not fail-closed** — an unrecognized drug silently falls through to the `LOW`/"safe to dispense" default. Fail-closed only exists one layer up, in `HttpTriageClient.java`'s wrapper (`UNKNOWN` never `LOW` on any failure/timeout/unrecognized response). **mcp-agent talks to triage-service directly, bypassing that Java wrapper entirely** — so today there is no fail-closed protection on that path at all; `tools.py` defaults to the string `"UNKNOWN"` only on parse failure, and nothing stops the LLM from recommending dispense anyway. This is a more concrete version of the "output safety" gap than the handoff doc's framing — worth having in view for M1.
- **PHI redaction has a real precedent to copy**: `provider-registry-service`'s `sanitize_location()` + structural (not scrub-after-the-fact) logging middleware. There's also a documented near-miss (`docs/developer-guide.md`): a design doc claimed a PHI-safety mechanism existed for five milestones before anyone checked — it didn't. Direct caution against writing "PHI-redact span attributes" in a plan without verifying it's wired.
- **A live, currently-open PHI exposure already exists**: Kong's `file-log` plugin logs raw request URIs (containing patient/member IDs) to stdout today, per `docs/gateway-runbook.md`'s own acknowledgment. Worth deciding whether Phase 5's observability/redaction work touches this opportunistically.
- **Timeout convention across the deterministic tier is consistent**: explicit connect-timeout + overall-timeout pairs (5s/20s), and a timeout is folded into the *same* fail-closed branch as any other failure — never a special "assume okay" path. `HttpTriageClient.java` explicitly defers circuit breakers as future work ("changes latency, not policy"). mcp-agent today has one flat 30s timeout, no distinct connect timeout, no retry. If M4 wants a circuit breaker in front of the LLM API, that's a new pattern relative to repo precedent, not an extension of one.
- **Every existing rate limiter in the repo (Kong's `fhir-rate-limit`, provider-registry-service's in-process limiter) is fail-closed/block-over-limit (429).** None "alert without shedding." The plan's M4 proposal to alert-not-shed on the LLM call is a genuine departure from every precedent here — and arguably in tension with its own "never silently drop a care request" framing, since alert-only means the request still goes through uncapped. That needs an explicit rationale, not an implicit one.
- **No single error-shape convention exists to inherit** — FHIR `OperationOutcome` (claims-service, epic-emulator, fhir-service) vs. plain FastAPI `{"detail": ...}` (triage-service) vs. structured `{error_type, message}` (provider-registry-service) are three unreconciled shapes. M1's output contract needs to pick one deliberately and say why, not assume there's a repo standard.

## Other facts worth having before any milestone doc

- **claims-agent already has a `--no-llm` deterministic mode** (template-rendered explanation, no API key needed) that mcp-agent lacks — a real existing fallback pattern, potentially relevant to M1/M6's fail-closed design, that the handoff doc didn't mention.
- **Neither agent has any provider abstraction, memory persistence, or observability today** — both are equivalently minimal Anthropic-only scripts. The "carry to Phase 2's claims stack" premise is architecturally sound (nearly identical skeletons), but there's no existing asymmetry to exploit — it's a clean build for both.
- **Gateway-level observability is not a clean slate**: Kong's Prometheus plugin and a GKE-Managed-Prometheus `ServiceMonitor` are already declared (though not confirmed scraped) — but only on the Phase 1 KIC deployment, not the Phase 2 docker-compose Kong that fronts triage/claims locally, and not at the application/LLM level anywhere. M2 should probably feed that existing pipeline rather than stand up a parallel one.
- **The `oneOf`-schema-fragility memory concern doesn't apply to any tool schema that exists today** — both current tools (`get_patient_summary`, `assess_refill_risk`) are flat single/dual-string-param schemas with zero nesting. It's a forward-looking concern for whatever M1's enum-output tool or M5's cross-provider schemas end up shaped like, not a current bug to fix.

## What needs to be discussed (merging the handoff's §8 with what the audit surfaced)

1. **Phase numbering and the epic-emulator collision** (new, and probably the highest-priority one — it affects the branch/doc structure of everything else).
2. Relationship to the open pagination safety bug — block Phase 5 on it, run in parallel, or explicitly out of scope with a stated reason.
3. Enum set for the pilot surface + REVIEW semantics — now informed by `claims-service`'s existing `Severity`/`Outcome` vocabulary; decide whether to reuse it or diverge deliberately.
4. Whether the "alert not auto-shed" rate/cost control is intentional given it contradicts every existing rate-limiter's fail-closed posture.
5. Error-shape choice for the agent's fail-closed output (FHIR `OperationOutcome` vs. `{error_type, message}` vs. something new).
6. Whether M2 observability plugs into the existing (declared-but-unconfirmed) Kong/Managed-Prometheus pipeline or stands alone.
7. Whether to touch the live Kong PHI-in-logs exposure while doing PHI-redaction work, or leave it out of scope.
8. The rest of the original §8 list (session-store tech, "important" response definition, transport, RAG corpus, memory token-budget numbers) — unchanged, still open.

Convention observed: `phase1-v1` marks a snapshot taken *at a phase boundary*, not "phase complete" in the abstract. To match that pattern, `phase2-v1` and `phase3-v1` would need to be tagged retroactively at the actual merge commits where each phase's last milestone landed (found via `git log`, not just tagged at current HEAD) — before Phase 5 starts would be the natural boundary for a `phase4-v1`-or-whatever-it's-called tag, **except Phase 4 is explicitly not fully closed** (open safety bug), so tagging it as a clean boundary right now would recreate the exact status-truthfulness problem in a git tag instead of a doc.

Later refined by the fail-closed decision (below), which changed how an *unavailable* triage is interpreted — not the reuse boundary itself. |

# Decision Index (ADR-style)

Every architectural decision on this project, in one auditable list: what was decided, its
status, what superseded it, and where the full rationale lives.

**This page is an index, not a rewrite.** Each decision's reasoning already exists in a
normative document; duplicating it here would create two versions that drift. Follow the link
for the *why*. Read this page for *what was decided, and whether it still holds*.

Two families:

- **D1–D8 — Deviations from the source PRD.** Where what we agreed to build differs from the
  DRAFT PRD. Full table: [`requirements.md` → Deviations](./requirements.md#deviations-from-the-prd).
- **C1–C4 — Cloud, security & scalability decisions.** Made during design, before build. Full
  table: [`README.md`](./README.md).

Status values: **Accepted** (in force) · **Superseded** (replaced — successor named) ·
**Partially delivered** (accepted, but the repo does not yet match — the gap is named).

---

## D — Deviations from the PRD

| # | Decision | Status | Notes / supersession |
|---|---|---|---|
| **D1** | **Hybrid rules stack** — new adjudication rules in Java; **reuse** the Python `triage-service` for drug-allergy + duplicate-therapy rather than rebuilding in Java | ✅ Accepted | In force and load-bearing. Later refined by the fail-closed decision (below), which changed how an *unavailable* triage is interpreted — not the reuse boundary itself. |
| **D2** | `rxclaim-emulator` is its **own top-level module**, a *sibling* to the EHR emulators, not a member | ✅ Accepted | Enforced in the tree and restated in [`epic-emulator`](../../epic-emulator/README.md) / [`athena-emulator`](../../athena-emulator/README.md) non-goals. |
| **D3** | A **separate `claims-agent`**, not an extension of the Phase 1 `mcp-agent` | ✅ Accepted | Protects R9. The two agents share only non-clinical plumbing. |
| **D4** | **Edge Kong** fronting claims+fhir+triage; emulator strictly private; **opt-in** DB-less Kong compose profile; **hybrid gateway** with a strangler migration | ✅ Accepted | Operational detail now consolidated in the [gateway runbook](../gateway-runbook.md). Refined by **C2**, which chose the DB-less dialect as canonical. |
| **D5** | **Canonical scope:** 15–20 rules / ~8 domains; **4–5 paths** exercised end-to-end | ✅ Accepted | Resolved three conflicting PRD numbers. Per-service Cloud Run stubs shipped for the two Java services (M2, M3); the top-level root module, `deploy-phase2.sh`, `claims-agent`'s config, and the cloud smoke test never did. See the [cloud-delivery gap](./plan.md#6-workstreams--milestones) and [§16 item 9](./plan.md#16-future-work). |

## 4. Recommendations for Phase 5 (and one thing before it)

### 4.0 Before Phase 5 starts: fix or mitigate §1.1

This is a live safety-relevant bug in merged code, not a Phase 5 backlog item. Two real fix
options, not mutually exclusive:

1. **The durable fix:** make `client/clinical`'s FHIR client follow `Bundle.link[relation=next]`
   when fetching medications/allergies. This is the correct behavior against *any* real FHIR
   server, not just `epic-emulator` — Phase 4 only surfaced a pre-existing latent gap in Phase 1
   code, it didn't create the underlying assumption. This does touch `triage-service`'s dependency
   (`client/clinical`), which is more invasive than anything Phase 4 itself touched.
2. **The fast mitigation:** raise `epic.quirks.pagination.max-count`'s default well above any
   realistic patient record count (or make quirk A's cap configurable per-deployment with a safe
   default), so the emulator's own demonstrability doesn't come at the cost of plausible patients
   silently losing data. This doesn't fix the underlying client gap (a real Epic server could still
   paginate at a value the client doesn't expect) but closes the immediate hole.

**This wasn't fixed as part of this analysis — it's flagged for an explicit decision** on priority
and approach before treating Phase 4 as fully closed.

### 4.1 Testing policy: add consequence-level tests, not just mechanism-level ones

For any quirk or backfill that changes response *shape or content*, require at least one test that
exercises it through the same client code path a real consumer uses (as `e2e/
test_epic_emulator_acceptance.py` already does for the happy path) with a realistic *volume* of
data, not just a realistic *shape* of data. §1.1 would have been caught by a 25-allergy fixture in
the existing e2e test.

### 4.2 Wire epic-emulator into CI

At minimum: a `phase4-java` job running `mvn -f epic-emulator/pom.xml test` on every PR (mirroring
`phase2-java`/`phase3` conventions already established), so this module's own test suite — once
§4.1 closes the coverage gap — actually runs automatically instead of depending on a developer
remembering to.

### 4.3 Decompose auth first, if/when Phase 5 decomposes at all

Per the coupling note: auth is evidence-backed as the cleanest split. Extension handling and
pagination should stay together unless a real pipeline contract is designed first. Error-shape
formatting needs an explicit home (shared library, or its own small service) rather than being
implicitly owned by "whichever area happened to build it first."

### 4.4 Resolve E10 if real Epic access ever becomes available

Every quirk/extension specific value in this module remains an unverified, structurally-plausible
placeholder (decision E10). If a future effort gets real Epic sandbox or documentation access, this
is the one item that would most change what's actually built here — including, possibly, the exact
pagination cap value that made §1.1 possible in the first place.

### 4.5 Update the demo guide, once §4.0 is resolved

Don't add Phase 4 to `docs/demo-guide.md` until §4.0 has a resolution — a demo built on the current
pagination behavior risks reproducing §2.3's exact scenario in front of a real audience.
